{{Short description|Mathematical measure invariant under linear isometries}}
{{Orphan|date=March 2017}}

In [[probability theory]], an '''isotropic measure''' is any mathematical [[Measure (mathematics)|measure]] that is invariant under [[Isometry#Linear isometry|linear isometries]]. It is a standard simplification and assumption used in probability theory. Generally, it is used in the context of [[Measure (mathematics)|measure theory]] on <math>n</math>-dimensional [[Euclidean space]], for which it can be intuitive to study measures that are unchanged by rotations and translations. An obvious example of such a measure is the standard way of assigning a measure to [[subset]]s of ''n''-dimensional Euclidean space: [[Lebesgue measure]].

== Definition ==
An '''isotropic measure''' on <math>\mathbb{R}^{d}</math> is a ([[Borel measure|Borel]]) measure that is [[Absolute continuity#Absolute continuity of measures|absolutely continuous]] on <math>\mathbb {R}^d \smallsetminus \{ 0 \}</math> and that is invariant under [[Isometry|linear isometries]] of <math>\mathbb{R}^{d}</math>.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Bogdan|first=Krzysztof|last2=Grzywny|first2=Tomasz|last3=Ryznar|first3=Michał|date=2014-06-07|title=Barriers, exit time and survival probability for unimodal Lévy processes|journal=Probability Theory and Related Fields|language=en|volume=162|issue=1–2|pages=155–198|doi=10.1007/s00440-014-0568-6|issn=0178-8051|arxiv=1307.0270}}</ref> Alternatively, an isotropic measure, <math>\mu(dz)</math>, is a measure for which there exists a real [[Probability density function|density function]] <math>\mu_{0}(r)</math> on <math>(0,\infty)</math> such that <math>\mu(dz) = \mu_{0}\left( |z| \right)dz</math> for <math>z \neq 0</math>.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Toshiro|first=Watanabe|year=1983|title=The isoperimetric inequality for isotropic unimodal Lévy processes|journal=Z. Wahrsch. Verw. Gebiete|volume=63 |issue=4|pages=487–499}}</ref>

== Example ==
* The [[Lebesgue measure]] on <math>\mathbb{R}^{d}</math> is invariant under [[Isometry|linear isometries]] and is hence an isotropic measure. In this case, <math>\mu(dz) = dz</math>.
* For <math>d=1</math>, the linear isometries of <math>\mathbb{R}^{1}</math> are of the form <math>f(x) = x + c</math> or <math>f(x) = -x + c</math>, for some constant <math>c \in \mathbb{R}</math>. Hence an isotropic measure on <math>\mathbb{R}^{1}</math> must satisfy <math>\mu(A) = \mu(-A + b)</math>, for any <math>A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{1}</math> and <math>b \in \mathbb{R}</math>. The measure <math>\mu(dz) = |z|^{-2} dz</math>, for <math>z \neq 0</math>, is one such isotropic measure.

== Unimodal measure ==
In probability theory it is common that another assumption is added to measures in addition to the measure being isotropic. A '''unimodal measure''' (or '''isotropic unimodal measure''') is any isotropic measure <math>\mu(dz) = \mu_{0}\left( |z| \right)dz</math> such that <math>\mu_{0}(r)</math> is nonincreasing on <math>(0,\infty)</math>. It is possible that <math>\mu\left( \left\{ 0 \right\} \right)>0</math>.<ref name=":1" />

== Isotropic and unimodal stochastic processes ==
In studying [[stochastic process]]es, in particular [[Lévy process]]es,<ref>{{Cite book|title=Lévy processes and infinitely divisible distributions|last=Sato|first=Ken-iti|date=1999-01-01|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0521553025|oclc=41142930}}</ref> a reasonable assumption to make is that, for each element of the index set, the probability distributions of the [[random variable]]s are isotropic or even unimodal measures.

More specifically, an '''isotropic Lévy process''' is a [[Lévy process]], <math>X = \left( X_t, t \geq 0 \right)</math>, such that all its [[Probability distribution|distributions]], <math>p_{t} (dx)</math>, are isotropic measures.<ref name=":0" /> A '''unimodal Lévy process''' (or '''isotropic unimodal Lévy process''') is a [[Lévy process]], <math>X = \left( X_t, t \geq 0 \right)</math>, such that all its distributions, <math>p_{t} (dx)</math>, are unimodal measures.<ref name=":0" />
